From Middle English fence, fens, short for defence, defens (“the act of defending”), from Old French defens, defense (see defence). The sense "enclosure" arises in the mid 15th century. Also from the 15th century is use as a verb in the sense "to enclose with a fence". The generalized sense "to defend, screen, protect" arises ca. 1500. The sense "to fight with swords (rapiers)" is from the 1590s (Shakespeare). Displaced native Old English heġe (compare Modern English hedge).

senses.d: A thin artificial barrier that separates two pieces of land or forms a perimeter enclosing the lands of a house, building, etc.
ex: There was a weak place in the fence separating the two inclosures

senses.d: Someone who hides or buys and sells stolen goods, a criminal middleman for transactions of stolen goods.

senses.d: A guard or guide on machinery.

senses.d: A prohibition enacted to prevent violation of another more primary rule.
A memory barrier.
The boundary.
To enclose, contain or separate by building fence.
ex:
[…] pray you, if you know,
Where in the purlieus of this forest stands
A sheep-cote fenc’d about with olive trees?

[…] O thou wall,
That girdlest in those wolves, dive in the earth,
And fence not Athens.

senses.d: To defend or guard.
ex:
Cosin, our hands I hope shall fence our heads,
And strike off his that makes you threaten vs.

[…] I have learn’t
To fence my ear against thy sorceries.
